verdict.tagline: Deep tactical combat and sprawling quests, balanced by steep initial difficulty.
for_you_if: you enjoy deep tactical combat relying on elemental interactions
you want sprawling role-playing adventures requiring careful positioning
not_for_you_if: you dislike punishing difficulty and steep learning curves
you struggle with confusing quest logs lacking direct guidance
you experience multiplayer disconnects or synchronization bugs

cohorts.label: 2-20h
cohorts.summary: Initial encounters feel punishing and lack direct guidance, while multiplayer sessions experience technical bugs and combat relies heavily on positioning and elemental surfaces.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the early game and initial combat encounters are excessively difficult, punishing, or feel unfair.

citations.review_text: The combat is considered hard but it isn't that, it's unfair. You start with nothing, no armour and rubbish weapons and pretty soon you are up against magic armour which blocks most of your good spells and strong weapons. You start every fight in a clustered group and immediately get hit by a burning or blinding attacks which affects all part members. There is little healing around. The story isn't anywhere near interesting enough (it might be later) to motivate you to slog through the pain. Avoid.

Game is fun but imbalanced.  Very hard starting out in classic mode, you almost die in every fight.  I had to ruin the storyline and kill random npcs because equipment was so hard to obtain, simply not to die in 2 rounds.  Also dislike that characters are prebuilt.  Mods are unfortunately needed for a better experience.

Entirely too difficult at early levels. Not enough armor/gear to stand a chance in any fight, even with cheese tactics and Classic mode. There's a fine line between a challenging learning curve and BS. I've been playing RPGs for years and this just is NOT enjoyable to play. Hard pass.

Game suffers from the same problem as the first one: combat is absolutely sh|t.
-unfair, overpowered enemies
-forced to play a certain playstyle
-no freedom of choice
-enemies have always way more AP than you do
-whoever thought this was a good idea to leave it the way it is deserves the worst fate possible to befall them
This game is not for people new to the genre. I was excited for the voiced story but even on the lowest difficulty it's way too hard without looking up guides.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game lacks a hand-holding tutorial or clear objectives, requiring players to figure out mechanics and direction on their own.

citations.review_text:
if you liked bg3, youll like dos2. this is the mindset i came out with after playing this game
charming characters. great narration. amazing story. allows for a surprising amount of creative thinking if you put your mind to it, and is hands down one of larians best works
you may need a tutorial or two. thats fine. maybe this is just me being mediocre at games. its still fun though and i could play this game for a day straight if i could. super addicting and replayable

I appreciate the animations and depth of the game.
However, I play singleplayer games to have an easy and fun experience, i have spent 3 hours in this game and double that trying to figure out what i'm supposed to do. 
If you like figuring out everything by yourself without a clear objective then this is perfect for you.

This is a great game. I'm not even finished with act 2 yet and I know this. It is a unique spin on the typical fantasy tales with some ambitious choices in design that make the experience new and exciting. The story definitely doesn't hold your hand at all and combat is something that requires serious thought. If you are just starting out, I do personally recommend beginning a campaign on explorer mode. Learn the games mechanics, immerse yourself in the world. Have fun :)
This game makes no sense, it's barely impossible to understand without any prior knowledge of all the mechanics

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat system as heavily reliant on positioning, environmental surfaces, and elemental interactions.

citations.review_text: It's a good game, with great writing, character depth, and such a vivid world. From the moment the boat goes binted (they like to start their games this way), you will love exploring and looking at the world around you - and it rewards exploration as well. I already know there are things I've missed that I'll discover on the second, third etc. plays through. The combat is also pretty good, but can be very unforgiving, and you really want to pay attention to surfaces, clouds, element interactions and such. Or just fill a crate with as much heavy stuff as you can, and use TK to throw it at enemies because it's perfectly balanced.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 – Definitive Edition is a benchmark modern CRPG built on systemic freedom, reactive world design, and highly flexible character building. Nearly every encounter can be solved in multiple ways combat, environmental manipulation, dialogue, stealth, or combinations of all three; making experimentation a core part of the experience.

Turn-based combat is deep and highly tactical, with strong emphasis on elemental interactions and positioning. The class system is deliberately loose, allowing hybrid builds that can drastically change how a playthrough unfolds. The writing and quest design are generally strong, often supporting multiple resolutions based on player choice.

It is also a demanding game in terms of time and attention. Inventory management, system complexity, and encounter difficulty can feel overwhelming for new players, especially in higher difficulties or solo play.

Highly recommended.

citations.review_text: good but divinity original sin enhanced edition had better Visual, Aesthetics, Map and Overall it is fun to play. PS: Some achievements in multiplayer don't work at the beginning of the game.

only play it a little with some friends, multiplayer was a buggy nightmare, no thank you, not sure how it was awhile back but in the current state i would not recommend this nonsense for any multiplayer endeavor multiple d/c , sync issues, and a whole lot of game breaking bugs pass.

cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: The steep learning curve gives way to deep strategic combat, though confusing quest logs continue to cause missed progress.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a steep learning curve and high difficulty, requiring familiarity with its challenges.

citations.review_text:
After nearly 80 hours, I finally finished a single playthrough, and what a playthrough it was. I acquired this game a long time ago, but after having enjoyed Baldurs Gate 3 so much, I decided to go back to it and see what it would be like. I wish I had tried it sooner!

That said, you're here for a review to see whether or not you should buy this. I'll not mince words, this game is difficult, and not just in terms of combat. There are many puzzles, quests do not hold your hand or directly guide you, and you can easily find yourself wandering into areas or encounters that are beyond your current level and ability. If that puts you off, I don't recommend this game for you. 

If you are wanting a CRPG that is challenging, but provides a large degree of freedom in how you do things, then I highly recommend this game for you. The game almost wants you to find creative ways to solve it, or break it. Sometimes when you play modern games you may get a voice in your head that tells you to do things in games "the right way", but in Divinity you are encouraged and rewarded for thinking outside the box, and that is particularly refreshing.
Great mechanics and super fun to play, but has a learning curve
Good game, DIFFICULT until you're familiar with the challenges.

I am playing this game after BG3, where I have over a thousand hours. I can definitely see some of the quality of life stuff in BG3 that are missing in this older/different game. That said, it is a different game and definitely not a D&D 5e sort of game. While the learning curve is steep, I'm starting to like this game and it is giving me the rush I had when I first played BG3 and every new place, encounter, hidden chest was something new and exciting. I think I'll come to love this game as much as BG3.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat system as strategic and deep, highlighting mechanics involving elemental surfaces and environmental interactions.

citations.review_text: Awesome game. I used to believe that I couldn't enjoy turn based combat but this game proved me wrong. I picked it up after hearing so much good about it. I don't regret it at all. There is incredible love for detail, sense of humour, cool game mechanics like the elemental surfaces/clouds and all you can do with it.
Larian's turn-based strategy formula is engaging and unique, something like mutant year zero with elemental reaction. Nicely done Larian.

I bought this thinking I'd spend a weekend on it.

Several hours later, I'm still finding quests I somehow missed, NPCs I accidentally got killed, and creative ways to completely derail Larian's carefully crafted plans.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 doesn't just let you make choices, it *dares* you to. Want to talk your way through a problem? Go for it. Want to sneak around? Easy. Want to teleport a heavily armored knight into a pit of lava while your skeleton friend picks someone's pocket? The game just shrugs and says, "Yeah... that works."

Every fight feels like a puzzle instead of a stat check. Fire spreads. Oil explodes. Rain changes everything. The environment isn't just decoration, it's another party member that's equally likely to help you or ruin your day.

The writing is fantastic, the companions actually feel like people instead of quest dispensers, and the soundtrack has absolutely no business being this good. I genuinely felt like I'd gone on an adventure rather than simply playing a game solo or with the company of friends.

It's also one of the few RPGs where "I'll just do one more quest before bed" is the gaming equivalent of saying "I'll watch one more episode." Suddenly it's 3:17 AM and you're debating moral philosophy with a talking squirrel while your inventory resembles a medieval flea market.

If you enjoy RPGs that respect your intelligence, reward experimentation, and constantly surprise you, this is one of the best ever made.

10/10.

Now if you'll excuse me, I need to start another playthrough because apparently I *still* haven't seen everything.

An incredible game with so many possibilities to interact and manipulate the environment to your playstyle; for a 12 year old game, it doesn't just hold its own, it stands up above so much of the competition, it is understandable that Larian would be able to produce BG3, and I cannot wait for the next installment of the Divinity saga

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the quest log and design can be confusing, lacking direct guidance or readable clues and leading to broken or missed progress if actions are mistimed.

citations.review_text:
Larian shows once again that they can't write later acts and entirely frontload their games. Character writing IS good, but a certain choice made at the end of the first act means you don't get to see a substantial chunk of it, and the main plot isn't good enough to suffice.

The combat requires you to min-max; there's no room for experimentation since it just makes the game infinitely harder than specialising into one thing and doing the same thing each combat (CC, deleting armor). It's DULL. Add to that an immensely confusing quest log that doesn't explain itself at all and you have one of the worst experiences literally ever. Play BG3 instead they got to use an actually functional combat system there, or play Fallout 2. Just don't play this.

Divinity 2 has ambition, but its quest design is a structural disaster. The game leans heavily on nonlinear storytelling, yet fails to provide the basic scaffolding that makes nonlinear quests work: consistent logic, readable clues, and consequences that follow from player actions.

Many quests hinge on arbitrary triggers, talk to an NPC too early and the quest breaks, talk to them too late and the quest resolves without context. Some quests expect you to intuit solutions that aren’t hinted at anywhere, while others drown you in irrelevant information. It’s the worst of both extremes.

The world is interesting, but the quest flow constantly derails immersion. Instead of feeling like a role‑playing experience, it feels like debugging someone else’s half‑finished design document.

May be the worst CRPG of all time.

I played both Divinity 1+2 and Baldurs Gate 3 and let me tell you something

Larian games are unpolished diamonds, and they just dont know how to polish stuff

Please ffs hire proper UI/UX people for Divinity 3

Their obssesion with coop play makes everything from party control to inventory management slog that just sucks the fun out of their games.

Did i have fun playing those games? Yes. Could it be infinitly better if it was made by devs who actually played any other RPG before? Totaly, but its just not happening.

Trilion different ways to complete quests also mean Gadzilion ways things can go wrong from bugs to failing. Absolute nightmare for completionist because one wrong conversation or wandering into zone you re not supposed to will ruin your entire playthrough.

I suppose the game gets decent after you finish it 10x or something, honestly have no idea.

Its just too fiddly. Story overall is good and fighting etc all hit the mark, but theres just too many instances of look for this tiny hidden switch to unlock this trap door. It doesn't add to the story, only your frustration, as you waste time not doing anything other than searching rooms over and over, and consulting the internet a few times an hour.

cohorts.label: 100h+
cohorts.summary: Long-term players note that maps fill with chaotic elemental effects and armor systems can create damage sponges, yet trial-and-error exploration remains rewarding.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the physical and magic armor system as punishing or problematic, resulting in damage-sponge enemies on higher difficulties.

citations.review_text:
Awesome game with amazing characters, a great plot with plenty of intrigue and an interesting combat system with unique and fun skills. 
But the problem is the infamous magic/physical armour system. It quite literally cripples every fight. It looms over every single combat encounter, and if you play on difficulties classic + then be prepared to deal with the damage sponges that are literally every enemy. I still love this game, and I'm very excited for the next one. (Especially after Larian confirmed getting RID of the magic/physical armour system.)

Can’t recommend this more to people who want to get into CRPGS. The combat and how it engages with its environment is SUCH a treat. I don’t think I’ve ever played something that makes me think about my surroundings so much. The physical/magic armour system has a relatively low learning curve but still makes the tactical part fun and engaging without becoming boring. I also really enjoyed the story and characters.

Minor critiques mostly do come down to the story having some plot points that feel a little bit unrefined at times— there’s a driving force in the plot that has a bit of a hole in it— but honestly it didn’t affect the overall experience for me, and I think it can be fun to theorize around it. Characters are really well done, but your ability to form a dynamically evolving relationship with them can feel a little limited (which is something they vastly improved on in BG3). I don’t think either of these things are reasons not to play, though, as someone who likes to play games across several genres mostly for story and characters.

Excellent turn-based game. Complete sandbox, no limits to combat. Some of the best, if not the best combat of any game. On highest difficulty, enemies can be a bit spongy, but otherwise it is fantastic. If you already played BG3, the combat rule set is completely different and this game isn't as good story or graphics wise, but it is still excellent, you will just have to read quite a bit. It runs great and is nearly bug free.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that completing quests and progressing requires trial and error, as the game does not provide clear direction or hand-holding on the map.

citations.review_text: I don't like this game at first bc it lacks of clear instruction point on the map which im not used to but after hours of playing, it actually helps me to explore the world more profound, it's so fun to explore the world n the culture, also the mechanic of the game has alot of options to play, great game with affordable price

I keep replaying this game, enjoying the fort joy then quitting in act 2 or 3, only to later only remember the joys of act 1 and replay it again. The skills have annoying hidden subtext, for instance when I cast shackles with provoke I expect to be attacked then I am not. Moving characters into back stabbing position is hard without pressing on other things. When you sneak in combat enemies just stand then instead of looking for you. Having high initiative doesnt matter as some characters will always go first, one shotting my solo rogue build. Clipping on the outfits is the norm. Progressing quests can be unintuitive tedious trial and error, for instance on the lady vengeance the way to proceed is to find a book without being told that on a random body, when there are bodies everywhere....

...Why do I likem this game?!?!

It may take a while for newcomers to get used to the scale of games like Larian's Divinity or Baldur's Gate series, but once it clicks, it sticks. Give yourself the time to get used to the systems, and explore what these games have to offer in terms of flexibility and freedom of choice. There's no right way to play, and no wrong way to have fun. It's a big world, and Larian doesn't hold your hand. Characters can live fulfilling lives and become heroes, or die in the dirt like filthy peasants. [b] That's for you to decide. [/b] 

There's a rich story, with astounding attention to detail, and at times it can feel a bit overwhelming, but if you aren't feeling like it, don't fret, you can always just punch your way out of most situations.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that combat encounters fill the maps with elemental effects, surfaces, and fire.

citations.review_text:
fun magic system with the floor and air getting covered in some type of material.
unfortunately this often ends in the map completely on fire, but its still fun

also I know its controversial, but I actually really like the armor system

D:OS2 has one of the best combat systems of all time. The interplay of aoe effects, elemental effects, surfaces, and tons of specific nuances to each spell and all your position options, mean every turn involves nuanced optimization and decision-making. Above all else, this game is an environment to provide great combat encounters, but the exploration, progression, looting, and freedom of experimentation with quests are all great too. Lohse and Fane are the best companions.

This game was OK at first then becomes a bit disappointing.  Although the graphics and storyline are good, the combat is tedious.  Every major battle turns into an inferno of acid and fire, and relies on pixel-accurate positioning just to stand a chance.  Levelling up makes a huge difference to you party's power, so if you attempt any battle outside the proper sequence of encounters your party just gets obliterated, so I found that I was wandering around the map trying various battles until eventually you come across one that you can win.  Even then, after a while I ran out of winnable encounters so in the end I was just getting killed by every available encounter, and eventually just ran out of patience.
